title: A Parking Ticket Caught the Son of Sam
central_question: How did a parking ticket end the hunt for New York's most feared killer?
content_notes: Closed case: Berkowitz pleaded guilty on 8 May 1978 and was sentenced on 12 June 1978. He is alive, so he appears only as an anonymous rim-lit silhouette with no face or likeness (tag 'ILLUSTRATION · NOT A LIKENESS'). The shootings, the victims, any weapon and any crime scene are never depicted; the street is a generic Brooklyn street, not the scene. Victims and survivors are not named; the witness is a generic, unnamed silhouette; police are generic 1970s figures with no badges, patches or logos. His letters are mentioned but never quoted or shown. The 'demon dog' claim is presented only as a story he later admitted was a hoax. Ticket amount, street and car colour conflict between sources and are left out. No real photograph, newspaper, ticket, police or court material is imitated. No dialogue is invented. Legal status verified 2026-10-11.

lines.text: For a year, police couldn't catch New York's most feared killer.
Then he parked by a fire hydrant.
Six people were killed, seven wounded.
He wrote letters to police and the press.
He called himself the Son of Sam.
He later claimed Sam was a neighbour whose dog relayed a demon's orders.
Then he admitted it was a hoax.
July 31st, 1977. His last attack, in Brooklyn.
Nearby, a dog walker saw police ticketing a car.
It was parked by a fire hydrant.
Days later, she told detectives.
They checked every ticket written there that night.
One was for a car registered in Yonkers.
On August 10th, police waited by that car.
When its owner walked out, police arrested him.
The Son of Sam was David Berkowitz, a 24-year-old postal worker.
In 1978, he pleaded guilty to all six murders.
25 years to life, for each one.
New York passed a Son of Sam law against criminals profiting from their stories.
In 1991, the Supreme Court struck it down.
A year of terror, ended by a parking ticket.
Next: the pensioner gang that drilled into a vault in London.

claims.text: Police identified David Berkowitz through a parking ticket. After the last shooting (Brooklyn, 31 July 1977) detectives checked the parking tickets issued in the area that night; one, for a car parked too close to a fire hydrant, was for a 1970 Ford Galaxie registered to David Berkowitz of Yonkers, a 24-year-old postal employee. (The ticket amount, the street and the car's colour differ between sources and are not used.)
Between July 1976 and July 1977 a gunman shot people in the Bronx, Queens and Brooklyn: six people were killed and seven wounded. He was arrested on 10 August 1977.

In April 1977 a handwritten letter addressed to NYPD Captain Joseph Borrelli was left near a Bronx shooting, the first in which the killer called himself the 'Son of Sam'. On 30 May 1977 Daily News columnist Jimmy Breslin received a letter from him, which the paper published. (Letters not quoted in the episode.)
The shooting on 31 July 1977 in Brooklyn was the last attack (and the first in Brooklyn).

A local woman walking her dog near the scene saw police ticketing a car parked by a fire hydrant, and reported it to police a few days later. Her name is spelled differently in different sources; she is not named in the episode.
On 10 August 1977 police found his car parked outside his apartment building in Yonkers, waited, and arrested him as he came out to it (reports say as he left his home / got into the car).

FUN FACT: after his arrest Berkowitz claimed that a demon, speaking through his neighbour's dog, had ordered the killings. He later retracted it: a 1979 letter to his psychiatrist called it a hoax, and in 1980 interview tapes (used in the 2025 Netflix series) he said he made up the dog story.

On 8 May 1978 he withdrew an insanity defence and pleaded guilty to the six murders; on 12 June 1978 he was sentenced to 25 years to life for each murder, to run consecutively (the maximum then allowed).

FUN FACT: in 1977 New York passed the 'Son of Sam law', which sent money a criminal earned from telling the story of the crime to the victims. In 1991 (Simon & Schuster v. Members of the New York State Crime Victims Board) the US Supreme Court held that version unconstitutional under the First Amendment; New York later enacted a revised law.

Berkowitz remains in a New York state prison. He was denied parole at every earlier hearing (the 12th denial was in May 2024); in May 2026 he declined to attend his parole hearing, saying he was not seeking release.

Next case tease: over the Easter weekend of April 2015 a gang that included men in their 60s and 70s drilled through the wall of a safe-deposit vault in Hatton Garden, London; police recorded them boasting in a pub in Islington, and they were convicted in 2016.
